newsitem.title: USA: Florida told to describe specifics of tobacco case.
newsitem.headline: Florida told to describe specifics of tobacco case.

text.p: Florida was ordered Thursday to explain to each of 13 tobacco industry defendants named in the state's $1 billion Medicaid lawsuit what they did that caused harm to Medicaid recipients.

Special Master William Rutter told attorneys for the state that they had to provide the information by July 28, the day Palm Beach Circuit Court Judge Harold Cohen will begin a final round of hearings before the jury trial begins Aug. 4.
The state sued tobacco companies to recover the Medicaid costs of treating people with smoking-related illnesses.

Rutter also told Florida's attorneys to provide tobacco companies with the state's definition of a "safer cigarette." He said Florida should be able to provide this information from the case outline already provided to Cohen.
Defense attorneys claimed during a hearing before Rutter Thursday that the information was critical to the case against each tobacco company.

"We don't know what is a safer cigarette design," said Philip Morris Cos Inc attorney Stephen Krigbaum, adding that tobacco companies also want to know which company may have designed a "safer cigarette" that should have been marketed to smokers in Florida.

Krigbaum said after the ruling that the state had "tended to lump all defendants together, making their allegations murky and vague in the lawsuit. Now they are being required to supply specificity, which should shed light through the fog."
W.C. Gentry, an attorney representing Florida, said the rulings were unimportant.
"All they (defendants) have to do is open the exhibits and they will see what they did wrong, bad and could have done differently," Gentry said.

In hearings Thursday and Friday, Rutter was attempting to clear up unanswered queries for information so that nothing would impede the trial, one of 40 filed by states seeking to win money to cover the cost of treating people with smoking-related illnesses.
The trial was expected to last into January.
